chapter: Clarifications and portraits: Lester Young, Byas, Blanton, Ben Webster
title: Lester Young: his humor, Prez and Lady Day, and how the Army changed him
summary: Lester was funny without trying; the Army and gin left him nervous and paranoid.

story.theme_name: Drafted: musicians in the military and the war years
story.community_name: Drafted: service bands, USO shows and the war years

blocks.x: He was a sensitive, gentle person?
What was he like as a person, I mean other than that kind of generalization?
Well he was just fun to be around. Because anything he said was funny, you know.
He intended it to be that way?

No, just him. Like he -- during he and Billie Holiday's association on records, she named him Prez and he named her Lady Day. And he didn't know how, he wasn't aggressive enough to get a girl. So Billie Holiday would have to go out and get a girl for him, you know. But later on he came out of that shell and got married and had a son.
Was he a great deal different after coming out of the Army?

Yes, well see the Army broke him up. The Army was his undoing. He and Jo Jones. They both were inducted during the time we were making the picture, "Jamming the Blues". And they were appearing out at Joe Morrison's Plantation out on Central Avenue. And they had to leave there and go into the Army. And Lester just cried tears. Well Jo cried inwardly and when they left the band, Buddy Rich took Jo's

place. And I think they paid him three times as much as Jo was making. You know. So when Lester came out of the service he was nervous from the service, you know. And he carried a fifth of gin in his saxophone case at all times.
Which he had not done before?
No, his thing was smoking grass. But it made an alcoholic out of him.
He was a lot -- as I understand it, I never knew him well, I only met him, but I understand he was much more withdrawn and introverted and didn't talk much, right?
Yes, he was real paranoid after the war.
